full_title: REP. NICASIO M. ALIPING, JR., PETITIONER, VS. COURT OF APPEALS (FORMER 4TH DIVISION), BISHOP CARLITO J. CENZON, ARCHBISHOP SOCRATES B. VILLEGAS, SHEREE M. NOLASCO, MARIE A. BALANGUE, NONNETTE C. BENNETT, DR. TERESITA F. DE VENECIA, ANTONIO J. SUPREMIDO, JR., AND PASTOR GENER TANDOC, RESPONDENTS.
subject: Political and Public International Law
syllabus_topic: VIII. Constitutional Rights > B. Equal Protection
topics: Equal protection: a kalikasan directive aimed only at the impleaded respondent is not discriminatory
Intentional or purposeful discrimination required (People v. Dela Piedra)
Due process: opportunity to be heard; restriction not arbitrary or oppressive
Writ of kalikasan: liability for road construction, tree-cutting and earth-moving inside and outside one's claim
Santo Tomas Forest Reserve; Amliang dams and Bued River

other_subjects.subject: Political and Public International Law

other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VI. Special Proceedings and Writs > J. Environmental Cases (AM 09-6-8-SC) > 3. Writ of Kalikasan

doctrine:
**A directive in a writ of kalikasan judgment that permanently enjoins only the impleaded respondent from developing his claim within a forest reserve does not violate the equal protection clause.** This holds even if other residents and garden owners in the reserve are not similarly restrained, where the directive is a specific remedial response to an anthropogenic activity unique to him and proven to be a major contributor to the environmental damage. The others are not similarly situated: they were not impleaded, and they were neither accused nor proven to have engaged in comparable acts. Applying *People v. Dela Piedra* by analogy, unequal application is not a denial of equal protection unless there is an element of **intentional or purposeful discrimination**. A discriminatory purpose is not presumed; there must be a showing of "clear and intentional discrimination."

The same directive does not violate **due process** where it was the product of bona fide proceedings in which the respondent actively participated and had ample opportunity to be heard. It is also not arbitrary or oppressive when it restrains only the acts (bulldozing, leveling, earth-moving, road construction) found to have caused the siltation and degradation of the waterways. It is a "necessary restriction to prevent further damage."

A person established as responsible for the construction of new roads is accountable for the illegal tree-cutting and earth-moving that resulted from it, **whether within or outside his claim**. He may therefore be ordered to mitigate erosion and rehabilitate the damaged areas. Bare insistence that the roads were old logging roads cannot overcome evidence that they were newly built.
facts:
Proclamation No. 581 (July 8, 1940) created the Santo Tomas Forest Reserve in Tuba, Benguet. Its natural springs sustain three Baguio Water District (BWD) dams (the Amliang dams), which supply some 4,176 households in Tuba and Baguio City. The springs are also the headwaters of the Bued River, which supports the San Fabian River Irrigation System serving about 1,144 hectares of Pangasinan farmland. In April–May 2014, acting on a report of tree-cutting and excavation on Mount Santo Tomas, the CENRO found two new roads inside the reserve: 1.5 kilometers from Sitio Amliang to Sitio Pongayan and 1.14 kilometers from Sitio Pongayan to Sitio Bekel. The roads had no Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC), tree-cutting or special land use permit, or road right-of-way or excavation permit. About 306 trees and 455 saplings were cut, causing damage estimated at P10,314,531.40, and the earth-moving silted the tributaries of Amliang Dam 3. The CENRO tagged petitioner Nicasio Aliping, Jr., then Representative of Baguio City, as responsible; the roads originated from land within the reserve that he claimed.

The PENRO filed a criminal complaint under Sections 77 and 78 of PD 705. The EMB issued a Notice of Violation cum Cease and Desist Order on June 2, 2014. At a July 14, 2014 technical conference, petitioner admitted undertaking an excavation project within his claim without an environmental permit, and the EMB fined him P50,000.00 under Section 4 of PD 1586. The BWD attributed the turbidity of Amliang Dam 3 to the road construction around petitioner's claim and to small-scale mining. In a May 21, 2014 letter to the Tuba mayor, petitioner undertook to institute measures "to avoid further damage to plants, trees and the [dam]."

Respondents Bishop Cenzon and others, residents of Baguio City and San Fabian, Pangasinan, filed a petition for writs of kalikasan and continuing mandamus. They named petitioner, DENR officials, Tuba officials and the Tuba police, and complained of four activities: (1) petitioner's road construction with illegal tree-cutting and earth-moving; (2) illegal small-scale mining; (3) expansion of gardens and residences through tax declarations over reserve land; and (4) relay towers on the mountains. On September 30, 2014, the Supreme Court issued the writ and a TEPO and referred the case to the CA. In his return, petitioner admitted excavating within his 2.6885-hectare claim to improve an existing access road. He denied any road construction or tree-cutting outside his claim and said the roads were old logging roads.

On May 6, 2015, the CA found the first three activities proven and the fourth not proven. It granted the writs and made the TEPO permanent. Item 4 of its fallo ordered petitioner to (a) permanently cease and desist from developing or enhancing his claimed property (bulldozing, leveling, any earth-moving, improving the old building, building structures, road opening and concreting), (b) mitigate the soil erosion causing siltation of the Amliang dams, and (c) rehabilitate the 2-kilometer stretch from his claim down to the river by massive tree planting. His motion for reconsideration was denied on October 29, 2015. In his Rule 45 petition, he argued that item 4(a) violated equal protection, since hundreds of other residents with vegetable gardens in the reserve were not restrained, and deprived him of the use of his property without due process. He also argued that items 4(b) and (c) had no evidentiary basis.
issues: Whether item 4(a) of the CA decision violates petitioner's right to the equal protection of the laws.
Whether item 4(a) deprives petitioner of the use of his property without due process of law.
Whether items 4(b) and (c) of the CA decision have factual basis.
ruling:
**1. No violation of equal protection.** The Court conceded that item 4(a) is directed exclusively at petitioner and that no similar restriction was imposed on other residents, even though residences and gardens were recognized as potential contributors to degradation. But petitioner was the only resident impleaded, because the petition imputed to him alone a specific anthropogenic activity: tree-cutting and earth-moving from a road construction project. **Item 4(a) "is nothing more than a specific remedial response"** to earth-moving activities confirmed to be a major contributor to the siltation of the streams leading to Amliang Dam 3 and the Bued River. The others were never impleaded and were not accused of, "much less proven to have engaged in," comparable activities. Citing *People v. Dela Piedra*, the Court held that a violation requires "intentional or purposeful discrimination," which is not presumed. There was "simply no evidence" that the CA intentionally discriminated against petitioner. The directive was designed to remedy an activity unique to him, and the other residents are differently situated.

**2. No violation of due process.** The decision was "the product of bona fide proceedings in which petitioner actively participated"; he filed a return and testified through a judicial affidavit, so he had ample opportunity to be heard. Nor is item 4(a) arbitrary or oppressive. It enjoins only acts such as bulldozing, leveling, earth-moving and road construction, the same acts found to have caused the siltation and continuing degradation of the waterways. It is "a necessary restriction to prevent further damage."

**3. Yes, items 4(b) and (c) have factual basis.** Petitioner conceded causing earth-moving within his claim without an ECC or permits, and his May 21, 2014 letter amounted to an admission of damage. The CENRO memorandum and the judicial affidavit of a resident showed the two roads were new, and petitioner's return admitted that both roads connect to or originate from his claim and that he excavated to improve access to it. **Taken together, these circumstances showed that the roads were built "at the behest of petitioner—and no other"**, for his sole benefit. His claim that they were old logging roads rested only on his "bare insistence." Being responsible for the new roads, he is accountable for the resulting tree-cutting and earth-moving "whether within or without his claim."
disposition: The petition was DENIED. The Court of Appeals' May 6, 2015 Decision and October 29, 2015 Resolution in CA-G.R. SP No. 00029 W/K, which granted the writs of kalikasan and continuing mandamus, made the TEPO permanent, and ordered petitioner to cease developing his claim, mitigate the erosion, and rehabilitate the damaged 2-kilometer stretch, were AFFIRMED.

bar_questions.q: Residents downstream of a watershed reserve filed a petition for a writ of kalikasan against Lito and several government agencies. They alleged that Lito bulldozed two new roads from his claimed lot inside the reserve, cutting hundreds of trees and silting the creeks that feed a city's water dam. Lito filed a return, testified through a judicial affidavit, and joined the hearings. The court granted the writ and permanently enjoined Lito from bulldozing, leveling, any earth-moving, building structures, or opening and concreting roads on his claim. Lito argues that (a) the injunction violates equal protection because hundreds of other settlers with vegetable gardens in the reserve were not similarly enjoined, and (b) it deprives him of the use of his property without due process. Rule on both arguments.

alac.answer: (a) There is no violation of equal protection. (b) There is no violation of due process. Both arguments fail.
alac.legal_basis: A directive in a kalikasan judgment aimed only at the impleaded respondent is not discriminatory when it is a specific remedial response to an anthropogenic activity unique to him and proven to contribute to the environmental damage. Others who were not impleaded and were not shown to have done comparable acts are not similarly situated. Unequal application violates equal protection only if there is intentional or purposeful discrimination, which is not presumed. Due process is satisfied where the directive results from bona fide proceedings in which the respondent actively participated, and it is not arbitrary or oppressive where it restrains only the acts found to have caused the damage. (Aliping v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 221823, June 21, 2022, En Banc, citing People v. Dela Piedra)
alac.application: (a) Lito alone was impleaded because the petition imputed to him alone the road construction, tree-cutting and earth-moving that silted the creeks. The other settlers were not accused or proven to have done anything comparable, so they are not similarly situated. Nothing shows the court intended to single him out; the injunction simply addresses his own proven acts. (b) Lito filed a return, testified, and took part in the hearings, so he was heard. The injunction covers only bulldozing, leveling, earth-moving, construction and road-opening, the very acts that degraded the watershed. It is a necessary restriction to prevent further damage, not an arbitrary taking of the use of his property.
alac.conclusion: The permanent injunction against Lito is valid and violates neither equal protection nor due process.

bar_questions.q: Forest officers found that dozens of persons had cut trees without permits in a forest reserve. The prosecutor filed charges under the Revised Forestry Code only against Mayor Dante, whose excavation project inside the reserve was documented by a CENRO report and his own admission before the EMB. Dante moves to dismiss, arguing that charging him alone while others equally guilty were not charged denies him the equal protection of the laws. Will the motion prosper?

alac.answer: No. Prosecuting one person while others equally guilty are not prosecuted is not, by itself, a denial of equal protection.
alac.legal_basis: The unequal application of a law fair on its face is not a denial of equal protection unless there is an element of intentional or purposeful discrimination. A discriminatory purpose is not presumed; there must be a showing of "clear and intentional discrimination." The prosecution of one guilty person while others equally guilty are not prosecuted is not, by itself, a denial of equal protection. (People v. Dela Piedra, as applied in Aliping v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 221823, June 21, 2022, En Banc)
alac.application: Dante shows only that others were not charged. He offers no evidence that the prosecutor charged him out of a deliberate design to discriminate against him. Like the respondent in Aliping, he was singled out because there was specific evidence against him: the CENRO report and his own admission before the EMB. Without proof of clear and intentional discrimination, his equal protection claim has no basis.
alac.conclusion: The motion to dismiss will not prosper because Dante has not shown intentional or purposeful discrimination.

bar_questions.q: In a writ of kalikasan case, Rico admitted excavating within his claimed lot inside a forest reserve "to improve an existing access road." He denied cutting any trees outside his lot and claimed that the two roads running from his lot were old logging roads. A CENRO memorandum and a resident's judicial affidavit showed that both roads were newly opened, and Rico admitted in his return that both roads originate from his lot. Trees were cut along the roads, and the resulting erosion silted a public water dam. May the court order Rico to mitigate the erosion and rehabilitate the damaged areas outside his lot?

alac.answer: Yes. Rico may be ordered to mitigate the erosion and rehabilitate the damaged areas, including those outside his lot.
alac.legal_basis: A person established as responsible for the construction of new roads in a forest reserve is accountable for the illegal tree-cutting and earth-moving that resulted from it, whether within or outside his claim. Responsibility may be inferred from the confluence of circumstances, such as roads that originate from his claim, are designed to connect it to other places, are newly built, and coincide with his own earth-moving. A bare claim that the roads were old logging roads, unsupported by evidence, cannot be given credence. (Aliping v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 221823, June 21, 2022, En Banc)
alac.application: The roads are new, as shown by the CENRO memorandum and the resident's affidavit. Rico admitted they originate from his lot and that he excavated to improve access, which shows the roads were built for his benefit and at his instance. His claim that they were old logging roads rests only on his word. As the person responsible for the roads, he answers for the tree-cutting and siltation they caused, wherever the damage occurred. Directives to mitigate the erosion and rehabilitate the damaged stretch are therefore supported by the evidence.
alac.conclusion: The court may validly order Rico to mitigate the erosion and rehabilitate the damaged areas within and outside his claim.

notes: The CA case is cited as "CA-G.R. SP No. 00029 W/K" in the opening and the fallo, and as "CA-G.R. No. 00029 W/K" elsewhere in the decision. Petitioner's May 21, 2014 letter refers to "Amliang Dam 5" in the source, apparently a typographical error since the reserve has Amliang Dams 1, 2A/2B and 3. The decision does not discuss the procedural rules on writs of kalikasan (A.M. No. 09-6-8-SC); the Remedial Law heading is listed for context only.
